title: Periodic material cells of most negative Poisson's ratio with a stiffness floor (QV-Topo 1)
statement: A periodic cell of 40 x 40 square elements describes a two-dimensional material: every element is solid (Young's modulus 1, Poisson's ratio 0.3, plane stress) or void (Young's modulus 1e-9). The cell must have at most the cell's volume fraction of solid elements, a minimum feature size of 2 (every solid element in a 2 x 2 solid square and every void one in a 2 x 2 void square, wrapping around the cell), no point contacts, and its solid elements must form one connected piece that wraps around the cell in both directions (a connected material). QV-Topo 1 (checkers/topopt_check.py, standard library only) computes the homogenised stiffness tensor C (Voigt notation, engineering shear strain) by the energy method with periodic boundary conditions: for each unit average strain the periodic displacement that minimises the energy, solved by our own direct solver, the same digits on every machine. THIS IS A NUMERICAL MODEL of an idealised material. The score is the larger of the two Poisson's ratios of a uniaxial stress along the cell's axes, nu12 = -S12/S11 and nu21 = -S12/S22 with S the inverse of C, rounded up to 0.000001; a cell is refused when either Young's modulus 1/S11 or 1/S22 is below the floor 0.01 (one per cent of the solid's), so that a mechanism with no stiffness cannot score. Two-dimensional stability bounds Poisson's ratio below by -1. The headline cell: volume fraction 0.5.
submission: Text file: 40 lines of 40 characters 0 or 1 (the top row first). See checkers/topopt_check.py.
score: the larger Poisson's ratio of uniaxial stress along the two axes, rounded up to 0.000001 (smaller is better)
context: Materials that widen when stretched (auxetics, negative Poisson's ratio) absorb energy and resist indentation; their microstructures are a classic target of inverse homogenisation (Sigmund 1994; Larsen, Sigmund and Bouwstra 1997). Without a stiffness requirement the problem degenerates into mechanisms, so each cell has a stiffness floor; Poisson's ratio is measured as in a tensile test (uniaxial stress), so no symmetry of the cell is needed. No published value applies under these settings: every cell is a first entry. Our first entries start from Grima and Evans' rotating squares (squares turned alternately, joined at the corners), drawn on the grid and then improved by a local search.
references: O. Sigmund, Materials with prescribed constitutive parameters: an inverse homogenization problem, Int. J. Solids Struct. 31 (1994) 2313-2329
O. Sigmund, A new class of extremal composites, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 48 (2000) 397-428
